verdicts.missing_content: Viterbi decoding (max-product dynamic programming) and the forward-backward algorithm are foundational for CTC and historical ASR. Section 20.0.3 currently presents CTC decoding via greedy argmax and beam search but does not introduce Viterbi as the underlying DP framework. The book mentions forward-backward only in a single bibliographic line. A short callout in 20.0.3 introducing Viterbi (replacing sum with max in forward-backward) and citing the HMM lineage would tighten the conceptual bridge from classical ASR to neural CTC. Baum-Welch (EM on HMM) could also be referenced when contrasting CTC's gradient-based training with classical HMM EM training.

EM as a general missing-data framework is not explicitly named anywhere in the book even though three LLM-adjacent algorithms use it: HuBERT iterative k-means clustering (20.0.4, framed as 'bootstrap clustering' without naming it as EM), VAE training (referenced across 16 files but the ELBO/lower-bound argument is the same Jensen's-inequality move as EM), and the Baum-Welch lineage behind CTC (20.0.3). A short Appendix A callout naming EM as the general 'guess latent, refit parameters' loop and pointing forward to its three LLM-era instances (k-means in HuBERT, ELBO in VAE, expert routing in MoE) would unify three currently disconnected derivations. Lower priority: the IBM Model 3 statistical-MT case study itself is interesting history but tangential to LLMs.

verdicts.notes: All concepts (parametrized functions, supervised/unsupervised/RL/self-supervised, regression vs classification, MSE/cross-entropy, error vs loss, sigmoid/logit) are foundational ML basics already covered in Chapter 0 and Appendix A at equivalent or greater depth. The GPT-3 175B vs linear regression 2-parameter framing is a nice rhetorical device but the book's scaling-laws chapter (6) handles the same idea more rigorously.

One-hot encoding, bag-of-words, TF-IDF, padding, and the RNN unrolled diagram are all standard pre-LLM material that the book covers in Chapter 1 (foundations and text representation) at full depth. RNNs in particular are revisited multiple times before the transformer is introduced.

Underfit/overfit triptych, train/validation/test split, learning curves, and the error-vs-loss mismatch are all foundational ML hygiene already covered in Chapter 0 and revisited throughout fine-tuning chapters (16, 17). Nothing the four-slide deck adds beyond what is in the book.

Linear, activation, softmax, dropout, normalization layers, and the GPU/host data path are all PyTorch primer content covered in the new Appendix E (PyTorch mini-book) and Chapter 0. The slide gallery of activations adds no concept beyond what the appendix already presents.
Pure course administration: team-based project rules, GitHub repos, AI-tool policy, three-presentation cadence. Out of scope for a book.

Pure course administration: market-expectation contrasts, code-first pedagogy, project objectives, common pitfalls. Out of scope. The 'five-question lens' for introducing a concept (what it does, API, how to use, how trained, how extended) is a teaching device, not book content.

Pure course administration: proposal/interim/final presentation card templates, GitHub layout, README sections. The two worked examples (ABSA of course reviews, dog-breed recognition) are duplicates of patterns already in decks 1041 and 2041. Out of scope.
Generic project-management and presentation-quality advice (scope definition, prior-art review, model selection, experiment planning, visual storytelling). Out of scope for a technical book.

verdicts.missing_content: Slides 6 to 14 walk through a real iterative debugging loop for synthetic data generation with LLMs: naive batch prompt (slide 6) produces unnatural, repetitive reviews; fine-tuning the prompt and raising temperature (slide 8) does not fix it; generating one-by-one (slide 9) still lacks diversity; the working fix is per-course generated style and tone attributes (slides 10-13). This concrete failure-and-fix sequence for diversity in synthetic generation is a useful case study for Section 16.5 or 16.6 (synthetic data for fine-tuning) where the book currently asserts that attribute-conditioned generation produces diverse data but does not show the failure modes that motivate it. Slides 25-30 also show a clean reframing from binary sentiment to conditional multilabel regression with target aspect-score vectors as the generation prompt, which is a transferable design pattern.

Several of the eleven project framings encode production patterns that are not covered elsewhere as case studies. Two stand out: (a) Project 7 'Medical Interrogation' uses two role-playing LLM instances (patient and doctor) with similarity-based evaluation across interrogation rounds, which is a clean multi-agent evaluation pattern relevant to Chapter 28 (multi-agent) and Chapter 46 (LLM-as-judge). (b) Project 9 'Pharma-forum critical-issue detection' uses RAG over DrugBank and WHO Essential Medicines List for classification rather than generation, which is a RAG application pattern (RAG-for-classification, evaluated on MedInfo2018) that the book's RAG chapters do not currently illustrate. (c) Project 2 'Code Review Assistant' uses GPT-4.1 cross-language code translation as a synthetic data strategy when target-language training data does not exist, a clean LLM-as-data-augmentation pattern. None of these need full sections; each is a one-paragraph case study for the relevant industry/application sub-chapter.

verdicts.notes: Pure course administration for the GenAI vision/audio course. The discriminative vs generative vs conditional-generative taxonomy is standard and already covered in the book's generation chapters. Out of scope.

The dog-breed classification walkthrough (LLM enumerates classes, Stable Diffusion synthesizes images, HF Trainer fine-tunes a head) is duplicative of patterns already in the multimodal chapters. The eleven past-project gallery (slides 22-31) is mostly pure computer vision (floor plans, plant damage, room re-identification, abandoned-object detection in surveillance), which is out of scope for the LLM book. Truly skip.
